# Padhāna Sutta (Snp 3.2 (PTS Snp 74))

**ID:** Snp 3.2 (PTS Snp 74)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Padhāna Sutta
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul2.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Padhāna Sutta* ("Striving" or "The Sutta of Exertion") is the second discourse of the Mahāvagga in the *Suttanipāta* (Snp 3.2, PTS Snp 74) [Katre 1931; Lamotte 1988]. Formulated as an archaic narrative ballad composed in twenty-five *anuṣṭubh* stanzas, the text depicts the Bodhisatta Gautama engaged in intense ascetic striving on the banks of the Nerañjarā river prior to his awakening, where Māra approaches to dissuade him from his spiritual exertion [Katre 1931; Lamotte 1988; Levman 2014]. Scholars note that it serves as an immediate thematic and narrative continuation of the preceding *Pabbajjā Sutta* (Snp 3.1), with which it may have originally formed a single ballad [Katre 1931; Pande 1974]. The sutta famously enumerates the eightfold army of Māra—beginning with sensual desire (*kāma*), aversion (*arati*), hunger and thirst (*khuppipāsa*), and craving (*taṇhā*)—and concludes with Māra's lamentation and the parable of the crow, noting that Māra had pursued the Bodhisatta fruitlessly for seven years [Katre 1931; Gaffney 2003; Bingenheimer 2008]. Stanzas from the sutta are also cited in the *Kathāvatthu* [Hazra 1994].

 Related versions are also found in Chinese translation in the *Fo benxing ji jing* and the *Saṃyuktāgama* [Nakamura 1980; Bingenheimer 2008]. DharmaNexus identifies substantial cross-language alignments with the Sanskrit *Mahāvastu-avadāna* and the Tibetan *Lalitavistara* (D0095), alongside matches in the Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* (T 99 and T 100) [DharmaNexus]. Within Pali literature, the sutta is cited in the *Mahāniddesa* (Mnd 4, 8, 13) and *Cullaniddesa* (Cnd 11), and shares extensive passages with the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā*, canonical Niddesa texts, and various subsequent subcommentaries (*ṭīkā*) [DharmaNexus].
